extracted.intended_audience: lay first-aid providers, attendants, rescuers and general public (people giving emergency first aid)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical first-aid procedures for heat exhaustion/stroke, electric shock/lightning, and a wide range of wounds, bleeding, bruises, abrasions and sprains; intended as step-by-step guidance for non‑specialist attendants until surgical/medical help is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat exhaustion first-aid
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry patient flat and lay in shade. Loosen clothes at neck and waist; raise head and give (a) teaspoonful of essence of ginger in glass of hot water, or (b) half a cup of hot coffee, clear. Put him to bed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the primary immediate steps for heat prostration (weakened persons from overwork/heat). Emphasizes rest, shade, loosening clothing and simple warm stimulants. (Labelled 'First Aid Rule 1-3' under HEAT EXHAUSTION.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat stroke immediate rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Send for physician; remove quickly to shady place, loosening clothes on the way; strip naked and put on wire mattress or canvas cot if obtainable; sprinkle with ice water or dash it from a basin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are initial rapid actions (First Aid Rules 1–4) for true heat stroke (high temperature, unconsciousness). Followed by more cooling measures (see next items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat stroke cooling and friction protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Dip sheet in ice water and tuck it snugly about patient; sprinkle outside of sheet with ice water; rub body through the sheet with piece of ice; put piece of ice to nape of neck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friction of the body through the sheet is considered 'absolutely necessary' to stimulate nervous system and circulation and to prevent blood being driven into internal organs by cold applied externally. Continue until temperature falls near normal (~98.6°F), then put to bed with ice cap on head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat cooling on fever return
rubrics_metrics.description: If fever returns, repeat whole cold-water application process until temperature is controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple method: lay patient nude on canvas cot/wire mattress, bind ice to back of neck, have attendant pour ice water from garden watering pot. Continue cycles as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectal nourishment and stimulation in insensible heat-stroke patient
rubrics_metrics.description: While patient is insensible do not give anything by mouth; inject half a pint of milk and two raw eggs with a pinch of salt into the rectum every eight hours after washing out with cold water; two tablespoonfuls of whisky may be added if pulse is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If urine not passed spontaneously, draw it every eight hours with a boiled soft rubber catheter lubricated with glycerin or vaseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sunstroke types (heat exhaustion vs heat stroke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types: (1) Heat exhaustion (prostration) - pale, cool moist skin, feeble rapid pulse, lowered temperature (95–96°F), usually conscious. (2) Heat stroke - direct sun exposure, flushed face, noisy breathing, strong pulse, very high internal temperature (107–110°F), sudden complete insensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification guides treatment urgency: heat stroke is much more dangerous (30–50% mortality historically) and requires physician and vigorous cooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric shock — protect rescuer first
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect yourself from being shocked by the victim: grasp victim only by coat tails or dry clothes; put rubber boots on hands or work through silk petticoat; throw loop of rubber suspenders or dry rope around him to pull off wire, or pry him with a dry stick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid direct contact with a victim still in circuit; ideal safeguard is thick rubber gloves and shutting off current at station if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric shock — drag, do not lift, free from wire
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not lift, but drag victim away from wire toward the ground. When free from wire, hold him head downward for two minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If contact with live conductor persists, pull or pry using insulators; if possible cut power. The head-down hold is advised immediately after freeing from wire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assist heart after electric shock
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply mustard plaster (mustard and water) to chest over heart; wrap in blanket wrung out of very hot water; give hypodermic of whisky, thirty minims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These were recommended stimulant/constriction measures to 'assist heart to regain its strength' historically; modern practice differs, but document preserves suggested immediate measures when no advanced care is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial respiration technique for electric shock
rubrics_metrics.description: Induce artificial respiration: open mouth, grasp tongue and pull forward; assistants alternately raise arms upward to enlarge chest (one assistant), and another uses a rocking/compression method on abdomen/chest to force expiration and then release; repeat 12–15 times per minute for 1–4 hours or until breathing resumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed multi-person method: one at head pulls arms up for inspiration; one astride hips compresses and then releases over ~5 seconds for expiration; change hands holding tongue as needed. Continue long-term if necessary; keep body warm with hot-water bottles and blankets while assisting respiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat burns after electric shock
rubrics_metrics.description: If skin not broken, cover burn with cloths wet with Carron oil (equal parts limewater and linseed/olive oil). If skin broken, spread paste of equal parts boric acid and vaseline and bandage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat burn surfaces according to whether skin is intact or raw. Also emphasize cleanliness and cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial respiration as most valuable remedial measure in doubtful electric fatalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When in doubt about cause of arrest (heart vs respiration), artificial respiration should always be practiced for hours in doubtful cases; it is the most valuable remedial measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two tablespoonfuls of brandy or whisky in a cup of warm water may be injected into the bowel if hypodermic syringe unavailable and patient needs decided stimulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main objectives in wound care
rubrics_metrics.description: Three essentials in the treatment of wounds are: 1. The arrest of bleeding. 2. Absolute cleanliness. 3. Rest of the injured part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that avoiding contamination is primary; without surgical cleanliness, other steps are rendered useless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bleeding classification and response
rubrics_metrics.description: Bleeding is of three kinds: (1) From a large artery (spurting bright blood). (2) From a vein (steady dark flow). (3) General oozing (small vessels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type determines actions: arterial needs pressure/tourniquet and surgeon; venous needs direct pressure and snug bandage; oozing often stops but treat with heat, elevation and antiseptic wet dressing if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arterial bleeding first-aid
rubrics_metrics.description: Speed increases safety: put patient down flat; make pressure with hands between wound and heart until surgeon arrives, assistants taking turns. If arm or leg, tie rubber tubing tight about limb between wound and heart, or tie strap over handkerchief; for arm use a baseball in axilla or tighten a noose and twist to compress main artery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep limb and patient warm with hot-water bottles till surgeon arrives. Tourniquet methods are temporary—surgeon must tie the vessel. Do not maintain arterial occlusion more than necessary (see later guidance about time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Venous bleeding first-aid
rubrics_metrics.description: Make firm pressure with pad of cloth directly over wound, and with hands between wound and extremity (away from heart); tie tight bandage about limb at this point; keep limb and patient warm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venous flow is continuous, dark red and usually easier to stop; after half hour release bandage to check for cessation, and if circulation impaired, reapply more loosely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctured wound management
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract pin/tack/nail/splinter/bullet IF YOU CAN SEE BULLET; do not probe. Pour warm water and squeeze tissue to encourage bleeding; send for small hard-rubber syringe. If deep, plug with boiled absorbent cotton and snug bandage; if shallow, cover with absorbent cotton wet with boric-acid or carbolic solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syringe later to forcibly irrigate with carbolic solution when available. Deep punctures should be kept open for drainage; consider surgical opening and drainage to prevent inflammation and lockjaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stopping oozing bleeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply water as hot as hand can bear; elevate the part and drench with carbolic solution (1 teaspoonful carbolic acid to 1 pint hot water); bandage snugly while wet; keep patient warm with hot-water bottles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General oozing from abrasions usually not dangerous; hot water and antiseptic wet dressing encourage clotting and cleanliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of wounds to avoid infection (cleanliness protocol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare by boiling absorbent cotton and a nail brush five minutes; scrub attendant's hands five minutes in hot water with soap and brush; clean patient's skin well around wound; bathe wound with boiled cotton and boiled water until all foreign matter removed; cover with boiled cotton and bandage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large wounds may be closed with stitches; very deep wounds should be left partly open for drainage. Small punctured wounds should be kept open by pushing in strips of boiled cotton to secure drainage.

rubrics_metrics.name: When and how to suture if surgeon unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: If surgeon cannot be obtained within 24 hours and attendant is confident, stitch with boiled needle(s) threaded with silk or cotton, scissors and towel boiled; scrub hands and cleanse wound; place stitches entering/leaving skin ~1/4 inch from edge and ~1/2 inch apart; tie and cut ends; cover with boiled cotton and bandage; leave for one week if no pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Needle should not be thrust deeper than skin; keep instruments on boiled towel; remove stitches after a week using boiled scissors and clean hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using court plaster (adhesive plasters) as primary dressing
rubrics_metrics.description: Court plaster or plaster of any kind is a bad covering or dressing for wounds, as it may be contaminated and keeps in any infection and prevents drainage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer boiled cotton/gauze and bandaging that allows drainage when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent wound closing at the top before bottom (drainage principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wounds should not be allowed to close at the top before healing is complete at the bottom; if tendency to close at surface while still discharging, enlarge the external opening or pack with gauze daily to keep outlet open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining drainage prevents formation of sinuses and deep pus collections; enlarging opening may be done surgically or by packing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lockjaw (tetanus) risk management
rubrics_metrics.description: Wounds producing lockjaw should be thoroughly opened to the bottom under ether by a surgeon, remove all foreign matter and cut out or cauterize surrounding tissue; consider subcutaneous injection of tetanus antitoxin to prevent disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly important for puncture wounds and hand injuries from explosives; stresses surgical debridement and prophylactic antitoxin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bleeding from scalp first-aid
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut or shave hair over area larger than wound; clean thoroughly with carbolic-acid solution (1 teaspoonful to pint of hot water); put pad of gauze or muslin directly over wet wound and make firm pressure with bandage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For scalp wounds, stitches often effective and not very painful if done immediately; tie stitches loosely and space ~1/2 inch apart to allow drainage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment for bleeding from lungs or stomach
rubrics_metrics.description: Let patient lie flat and swallow small pieces of ice; take 1/4 teaspoon of table salt in half a glass of cold water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate coughing up bright arterial blood (lungs) vs dark blood vomited (stomach), but same immediate first-aid measure is advised here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bruise treatment (contusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bandage from tips of fingers or toes making same pressure all the way up; apply heat through the bandage over injury with hot-water bottles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial treatment: rest, splint if needed, cold compresses initially, later hot applications and rubbing with liniment or vaseline as pain/swelling subside. Cataplasma kaolini and ichthyol ointment suggested historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abrasions (scrapes) care
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply ointment containing 60 grains boric acid to the ounce of vaseline and cover with bandage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same ointment can be used on small wounds/cuts after first bandage removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sprain initial management
rubrics_metrics.description: Immerse in water as hot as hand can bear for half an hour; dry and strap with adhesive plaster if known, if not bandage snugly beginning from tips of fingers or toes and make same pressure all the way up as over the injury; rest and bed if ankle or knee is hurt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sprain = wrench/twist of joint with damage to membranes/ligaments; severe cases may be fractures or dislocations so seek surgical aid promptly. Use splint for immobilization when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and placement of splints
rubrics_metrics.description: Injuries near joints should have a splint made of thin board or tin, covered with cotton wadding and bandaged, applied by means of surgeon's adhesive plaster and bandage after wound dressed; in hand injuries splint applied to palm side and reach from finger tips to above wrist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Splints insure rest and prevent further injury; for lower limbs, keep patient in bed with leg raised on a pillow.

rubrics_metrics.name: General treatment for shock (from hemorrhage or injury)
rubrics_metrics.description: If patient is pale, faint, cold skin, nausea from blood loss or shock, strip of clothing, wrap in blanket wrung out of hot water, cover with dry blankets; heat feet with hot-water bags; keep head low; give two tablespoonfuls of brandy, whisky or other alcoholic liquor in half cup of hot water by mouth if patient can swallow; if much blood lost, inject a quart of hot water with a teaspoonful of common salt into the rectum via fountain syringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shock following accidents treated similarly to hemorrhage; improvement indicated by return of color and pulse strength. Use caution and seek surgical/medical help.
